title: Cedric Knows
part: PART TWO: THE TOLL OF ONE STORY

pages.text:
*From the Bridgewater Almanac: A boy who says he is not afraid is either a hero or a liar.*

The streetlamp hummed, a low, yellow buzz in the wet air. Cedric stood in the pool of light, his red waistcoat bright against the dark cobbles. He did not look like a boy who had seen a monster. He looked like a boy who had seen a mistake.

"You were down there," he said, and it was not a question. His hand twitched at his side, fingers curling and uncurling. "I saw you go down the steps. I saw you come back up. You were gone for an hour, Rue."

Rue wiped her hands on her raincoat. "I was only crossing the bridge. The other side is shorter for the doctor's house."

"Nobody crosses the old bridge," Cedric said, his voice thin and high-pitched. "It is forbidden. It is dangerous. If you do not tell me what you saw, I will tell my uncle the Mayor. He will send the constabulary. He will send the whole town."

"Right then," Rue said. She felt her heart beat in her ears, a loud, steady thumping. She looked at his boots. They were muddy. He had been waiting for a long time.
pages.image: A rainy street at night with a glowing streetlamp; a skinny boy in a red waistcoat looks nervously at a small girl in a mustard-yellow raincoat, who stands calmly with her hands in her pockets.

pages.text:
Rue looked up at him and smiled. It was a good smile, the one she had been practicing since spring, which worked well on mothers, on the doctor, and now, apparently, on the Mayor’s nephew.

"There is nothing there," she said. "Just damp. And some moss. And a very old bridge."

It was the first time in her life she had told a lie with a straight face. It felt strange, like wearing a coat that was too big. She said it again, softer. "Just damp, Cedric."

Cedric stared at her. He took a step back, his heel scraping on the stone. He looked terrified, Rue realized. He was more frightened than she was. He was frightened of the dark, and he was frightened of being the only one who knew, and he was frightened of her. She filed this away, tucked it under her arm like a parcel.

"Suit yourself," he whispered. He turned and ran, his slicked-back hair flying behind him. Rue watched him go, and felt a small, cold knot tighten in her stomach.
pages.image: A dark alleyway where a skinny boy in a red waistcoat runs away in fear, leaving a small freckled girl in a yellow raincoat standing still in the lamplight, looking thoughtful.

pages.text:
By Wednesday, the story had changed. Cedric climbed back onto the crate, his voice higher and more urgent. He claimed the troll’s eye glowed like a red apple in the dark. He insisted it had a tail, long and frayed like a rope. He declared it ate one sheep a month, and that it was getting bolder.

The circle of listeners grew. They leaned in, breath held, eyes wide. It was a good story. It was a dangerous story. And every time Cedric spoke a new, terrible detail, he glanced at Rue. He was daring her to contradict him. He wanted her to say, *No, he doesn’t have a tail.* Or, *No, he doesn’t eat sheep.* He wanted to win.

Rue sat on her bench, picking at a thread on her sleeve. She said nothing. She watched the faces of the other children, bright with fear and excitement. She watched Cedric’s face, tight with effort. She wanted to scream. She wanted to hug him. Instead, she said nothing, and the story grew a little larger, a little more terrible.
pages.image: A schoolyard scene where a skinny boy in a red waistcoat stands on a crate telling a dramatic story to a crowd of children, while a small girl in a yellow raincoat sits on a bench, looking troubled.

pages.text:
Under the chestnut tree, Perrin Fen was drawing a sheep in his notebook. He did not look up when Cedric’s voice drifted over. He just kept drawing, his pencil scratching softly against the paper.

"A troll who eats one sheep a month," Perrin said, his voice quiet and clear, "would have eaten every sheep in Bridgewater by now." He looked up. "I counted. There are exactly as many sheep as there were last year. And I checked the baker’s farm. He is still there."

The yard went silent for a moment. Then, a few children laughed. It was not a cruel laugh this time. It was a relieved laugh, the kind that comes out when you realize you are not in danger. Cedric’s ears turned red. He climbed off the crate, his face a mask of confusion.

Rue laughed. The sound bubbled up in her chest, warm and sudden. She leaned forward, her fingers tightening on the edge of the bench. She wanted to tell Perrin. She wanted to say, *It’s true, he’s kind, he has a toothache, he likes tea.* She opened her mouth. The words were there, right on her tongue. She closed her mouth again. Not yet.
pages.image: A quiet moment under a large chestnut tree where a thin boy in an oversized wool hat looks up from a notebook, smiling gently at a small freckled girl in a yellow raincoat who is laughing.

pages.text:
That night, the air under the arch smelled of wet stone and old paper. Rue climbed the steps, a tin of scones in her hand. She expected Hobb to be sitting by his humming kettle. Instead, she found him behind his bookshelf, his large grey-green face pale in the lantern light.

He had heard the shouting. The sound of the schoolyard, faint and distant, had come down through the stones. He looked small. He looked hurt.

"I am fine," he said, his voice rough. He moved to sit on his cushion, but he did not touch the scones. Behind him, on the wall, the moss was growing. It had formed a small, tight ball, dense and dark, like a knot that would not untie.

Rue sat down on the floor beside him. She did not say it would be alright. She did not say he should be brave. She just sat, and she waited, and she let him be quiet. The ball of moss stayed tight, but it did not grow.
pages.image: A cozy hollow under a bridge arch where a large, mossy troll with spectacles sits hunched behind a bookshelf, looking shy, while a small girl in a yellow raincoat sits on the floor beside him, holding a tin of scones.
